answer: No verified study in this search jointly estimates the causal effect of removing moving car lanes for bicycles on all-mode people throughput and total passenger travel minutes. The five closest papers estimate selected vehicle outcomes; three London papers are related evidence, not independent city replications.

studies.citation: Klingen, J.J. (2021), Natural Experiments in Environmental and Transport Economics, chapter 5: Bikes lanes, road safety, and congestion. VU Amsterdam PhD thesis. Chapter coauthors: Daniel Graham, Jos van Ommeren, Erik Verhoef.
studies.status: Published thesis; related work remains on author's working-paper list, not verified journal publication.
studies.pages: Printed 86–95: treatment, data, methods; printed 98 / PDF106: Table 5.5.
studies.design: Manhattan north/south area-direction weekly two-way fixed effects, July 2012–June 2016. Treatment: ability to traverse an area fully on a protected lane. Within-road taxi trips proxy speed and flow; roadwork window excluded.
studies.result: Area speed log coefficient −0.013 (SE .011); taxi flow +.007 (.028): both insignificant. Re-expressed approximate normal 95% intervals: speed −1.29% [−3.40,+0.86]; flow +0.70% [−4.68,+6.38].
studies.lane_removal: Not established: protected-lane classification is not a moving-lane-removal indicator.
studies.data_code: Full thesis downloaded. No linked public processed panel or replication code found in thesis, repository, author page or targeted searches. Raw TLC, CSCL and bike-route sources cited; historical coordinates require independent availability check.
studies.critique: Area aggregation addresses local rerouting, not all spillovers. Taxi share may change; selected trips and post-treatment trip weights change composition. Fixed effects do not prove parallel trends. No all-mode passengers or person-minutes.
studies.version_warning: 2020 conference draft reported positive street coefficients; current author summary mentions ~1% area speed reduction. Use explicitly dated thesis table, not an unversioned headline.

studies.citation: Schrauth, P. (2022), The Causal Effect of Cycling Infrastructure on Traffic and Accidents: Evidence from Pop-up Bike Lanes in Berlin. CEPA Discussion Paper 48. DOI 10.25932/publishup-55335.
studies.status: Working paper; SSRN version posted 2023, not verified peer-reviewed publication.
studies.pages: Printed pp.9–16 methods/data; pp.20–22 and Table1 results.
studies.design: 2019–2020 hourly monitoring; event study and TWFE; 23 treated sensors on six streets. Controls exclude within 1 km and match lane counts. Station×lockdown controls. Synthetic control concerns accidents, not speed.
studies.result: Table1 adjusted level speed −4.123 km/h; log speed −0.122, equivalent to −11.5%. Adjusted log vehicle volume −0.00540, insignificant. Abstract's 'percentage points' is imprecise log-effect wording.
studies.lane_removal: Explicit: car lanes replaced, including two-to-one and three-to-two conversions.
studies.data_code: PDF downloaded. Senate/VMZ supplied traffic records; no verified public replication package. Public geography/accident inputs are insufficient alone.
studies.critique: COVID and treatment coincide; station-specific lockdown adjustment cannot absorb every differential recovery. Few treated streets, incomplete sensors, per-lane averaging, nearby diversion. No cycling/transit person totals or journey time. Closest verified moving-lane-removal study.

studies.citation: Bhuyan, P., McCoy, E.J., Li, H., Graham, D.J. (2021), Analysing the causal effect of London cycle superhighways on traffic congestion. Annals of Applied Statistics 15(4),1999–2022. DOI 10.1214/21-AOAS1450.
studies.design: 75 treated and 375 control zones; 2007–2014; pre/post GLMM, propensity weighting, doubly robust estimator. DfT/LAEI traffic, road and socioeconomic covariates.
studies.result: Doubly robust ATT: AADT −7.026% [−9.684,−5.007]; speed +2.096% [−0.813,+4.704]. Speed statistically inconclusive. ATE differs from ATT.
studies.lane_removal: Broad early CS schemes, described as barrier-free lanes; no verified segment-by-segment moving-lane reduction treatment.
studies.data_code: Accepted PDF downloadable. Public source datasets cited; no verified processed panel/code package. Later related paper explicitly restricts study data.
studies.critique: Annual vehicle averages and zonal exposure are not corridor peak travel times. No-all-unmeasured-confounding and no-interference assumptions remain; route diversion and mode changes unresolved. Cannot convert reduced vehicle flow to increased total people flow.

studies.citation: Zhang, Y., Li, H., Ren, G. (2025), Analysing the role of traffic volume as mediator in transport policy evaluation with causal mediation analysis and targeted learning. Transportation Research A 192,104369. DOI 10.1016/j.tra.2024.104369.
studies.status: Peer-reviewed; publisher abstract/method snippets verified, full text access not verified.
studies.design: London CS observational targeted-learning mediation: separate direct speed effect and indirect effect through motor volume.
studies.result: AADT −9.2%; direct speed effect −2.0%, indirect +1.3%, small combined effect. These are distinct estimands from the earlier ATT and are not independent city evidence.
studies.lane_removal: Less vehicle space proposed as mechanism; no verified moving-lane-removal-only exposure.
studies.data_code: No verified public panel/code located; do not present as immediately reproducible.
studies.critique: Mediation requires stronger sequential exchangeability assumptions, including mediator–outcome confounding. Mechanism interpretation is useful, but does not measure total person-minutes. For policy total effects, do not mechanically adjust for post-treatment traffic volume.

studies.citation: Bhuyan, P., Jana, K., McCoy, E.J. (2023), Causal analysis at extreme quantiles with application to London traffic flow data. JRSS C72(5),1452–1474. DOI10.1093/jrsssc/qlad080.
studies.design: 450 observations; covariate-adjusted quantile causal model of AADT, 2007–2010 baseline versus2011–2014 outcomes; heavy-tail extrapolation.
studies.result: Treated 99.5th-percentile AADT effect +28.80% [19.27,40.13], Table2. This is a distribution-tail vehicle-flow contrast, not an individual trip delay or mean congestion effect.
studies.lane_removal: Same broad early CS context; no verified moving-lane-removal-specific coding.
studies.data_code: Data availability statement: request from Haojie Li, not public due privacy/ethical restrictions. No verified downloadable replication code.
studies.critique: A higher AADT tail can coexist with a lower mean; does not contradict earlier mean estimates. Annual-flow extremes are not hourly peak congestion. Small extreme-tail effective sample, model extrapolation and unmeasured confounding matter. Does not solve people throughput/time.

requested_additional_check.citation: Moran, M., Salman, M., Yabe, T. (2026), Heterogeneous impacts of protected bike lanes on bikeshare behavior across demographic groups in New York. npj Sustainable Mobility and Transport3,39. DOI10.1038/s44333-026-00107-2.
requested_additional_check.result: PSM plus station/month TWFE reports +379 monthly Citi Bike starts per station after protected lane installation, p<.001.
requested_additional_check.data_code: Data availability links raw Citi Bike and end-2024 NYC bike-network data. Article has no code-availability section or GitHub/Zenodo repository link; targeted author/title searches found no public code. Supplement download checked separately.
requested_additional_check.lane_removal: Facility ClassI and proximity within100m do not identify removed moving vehicle lanes. No lane-count-change variable in reported exposure.
requested_additional_check.critique: Bike-share starts only; neither all cycling nor net mode shift. Post-treatment station supply/e-bike composition, spillovers, historical network survivorship and heterogeneous staggered TWFE deserve checks. Date-shuffle placebo does not prove absence of unobserved confounding. Do not append379 to corridor people counts.

screened_out.citation: Younes et al.(2024), The traffic calming effect of delineated bicycle lanes. Journal of Urban Mobility5,100071.
screened_out.reason: Useful real April2022 Asbury Park pilot,9575vehicle trajectories,−21% right-turn average speed; nine parking spaces removed and lanes narrowed, no moving lane removed. Intersection calming is not journey congestion/allmode throughput. PDF downloaded.

screened_out.citation: Marqués et al.(2015), How infrastructure can promote cycling in cities: Lessons from Seville. Research in Transportation Economics53,31–44.
screened_out.reason: Network descriptive case and modal-shift evidence; not verified quasi-experimental allmode time/throughput effect of moving-lane removal.

screened_out.citation: NYCDOT(2014), Protected Bicycle Lanes in NYC.
screened_out.reason: Before/after corridor taxi speeds and counts, useful descriptive benchmark; no credible comparison design verified. Search indexed source but direct download404 on check; do not list as successfully downloaded.

screened_out.citation: NYCDOT(2010), Green Light for Midtown evaluation.
screened_out.reason: Pedestrianization with east/west taxi comparison, bundled intervention rather than bike-lane conversion. Search indexed source; direct download404 on check.
